nameStory: This little wildflower gets its name from the tiny backward-pointing spurs that extend from each flower like miniature horns. The 'gentian' part connects it to the famous gentian family, named after King Gentius of ancient Illyria who supposedly discovered the medicinal properties of these plants around 180 BC.
description: Spurred gentian is a small, delicate annual wildflower that stands just 4-16 inches tall in New England's wetlands and moist forests. Its tiny greenish-purple or light green flowers are easy to miss at first glance, but look closer and you'll spot the distinctive backward-pointing spurs that make this plant special. The smooth, square stems support small, glossy leaves and clusters of 2-9 flowers that bloom during the heart of summer.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny four-petaled flowers (⅓ to ½ inch long) in shades of greenish-purple or light green, each with a distinctive backward-pointing spur that extends past the green sepals - run your finger along the back of the flower to feel these little projections

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, hairless stems that feel distinctly square when you roll them between your fingers - this four-sided shape is quite unusual and helpful for identification

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, simple leaves (½ to 2 inches long) that feel smooth and glossy to the touch with no teeth along the edges and no hairs anywhere on the surface

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual plant reaching only 4-16 inches tall, often overlooked among taller wetland plants until you're looking right down at it

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Cone-shaped dry capsules that stick out noticeably from the flower opening and split open when ripe to release seeds

habitat: Look for spurred gentian in New England's wetlands, boggy areas, and moist forest floors where the soil stays consistently damp. It thrives in the cool, humid conditions of northern forests and is most commonly found in Maine, with scattered populations in similar habitats throughout the region.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in moist soil as temperatures warm, but the plant remains small and inconspicuous with just its glossy leaves visible.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season from July through August when the tiny spurred flowers appear in small clusters - this is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the cone-shaped seed capsules mature and split open, releasing seeds before the plant dies back completely.
seasonality.winter: This annual plant dies completely, leaving no above-ground trace until seeds germinate the following spring.

funFact: Despite being called 'green gentian,' this little flower is actually more closely related to tropical gentians than to the big, showy blue gentians most people picture - and those backward spurs are perfectly designed landing platforms for tiny flies that most other flowers ignore!
confusionNotes: The small, greenish flowers might be overlooked as just another unremarkable wetland weed, but no other New England plant combines those distinctive backward spurs with square stems. Remember: 'Square stems, spurred flowers' - if you've got both, you've found your gentian.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name 'green gentian' fool you into expecting the large, trumpet-shaped blue flowers that most people associate with gentians. This modest little plant represents a completely different approach to the gentian lifestyle, preferring wet feet and tiny pollinators over mountain meadows and big bees.
compareHints: Spurred gentian is the only member of its genus (Halenia) found in New England, making it unique among our local gentians. Unlike the showy fringed gentian or bottle gentian with their large blue flowers, spurred gentian's tiny greenish blooms with backward spurs are unlike anything else in the gentian family here.
